description: Full-length May 2027-format practice exam: 55 MCQ (55 min), 3 SAQ (40 min), DBQ (60 min incl. 15-min reading), LEQ (40 min); 3h15m total. Section IA is 47 bank questions (pool test) plus 8 exam-only questions carried inline in examOnly (Q1–8; Units 1–2 test pools are full, so no bank IDs exist for them).

books.section: Topic 1.4 Columbian Exchange, Spanish Exploration, and Conquest

primary_sources: Bartolomé de las Casas, A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies (1542)

options.misconception: The debate was about how Indigenous laborers were paid.
options.text: Whether Indigenous peoples should be enslaved or paid wages for mining labor
Whether Spanish treatment of Indigenous peoples was morally justified

options.misconception: Las Casas was mainly concerned with how missionaries communicated.
options.text: Whether Spanish missionaries should learn Indigenous languages

options.misconception: The debate was about European alliances, not Spanish conduct.
options.text: Whether Spain should ally with France against England in the Americas

rationales.A: Las Casas argued about cruelty and justice, not about whether miners should be paid wages.
rationales.B: Las Casas wrote to condemn Spanish cruelty toward Indigenous peoples, and his account fed the debate over whether conquest and the encomienda could be morally justified.
rationales.C: Learning Indigenous languages was a missionary method, not the debate Las Casas raises here.
rationales.D: France and England do not explain a 1542 Spanish text about Spanish conduct.
rationales.general:
1. Name what Las Casas is doing. He describes Spaniards acting like wolves toward gentle, peaceable peoples.
2. Ask what question that description raises. Whether such treatment can be morally justified.
3. Set aside the other options. Wages, missionary languages, and a French alliance are not the issue in the passage.
4. Match the debate. The passage feeds the Spanish debate over the justice of conquest and the encomienda.
Remember: when a writer condemns cruelty, ask what moral question the condemnation raises.

books.section: Topic 1.4 Columbian Exchange, Spanish Exploration, and Conquest

primary_sources: Bartolomé de las Casas, A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies (1542)

options.misconception: The abuses came from competition over furs.
options.text: Competition among European powers for control of the fur trade

options.misconception: The abuses came from African slavery in the Chesapeake.
options.text: The introduction of African slavery in the Chesapeake colonies
The establishment of the encomienda system in the Caribbean

options.misconception: Protestant missionaries caused the abuses.
options.text: The spread of Protestant missionaries into New Spain

rationales.A: The fur trade was a later rivalry among European powers, not the Caribbean system of the 1500s.
rationales.B: African slavery in the Chesapeake came later and in a different place.
rationales.C: The encomienda system gave Spaniards control over Indigenous labor in the Caribbean, and the abuses it produced are exactly what Las Casas describes.
rationales.D: Protestant missionaries were not the actors in New Spain.
rationales.general:
1. Name the situation. Spaniards are behaving like wolves toward Indigenous peoples.
2. Ask what system put Spaniards in that position. The encomienda gave them control over Indigenous labor in the Caribbean.
3. Check the dates and places. The fur trade, Chesapeake slavery, and Protestant missions belong to other times and places.
4. Connect the system to the description. Encomienda control produced the abuses Las Casas saw.
Remember: to find a cause, match the system to the time and place of the description.

books.section: Topic 1.4 Columbian Exchange, Spanish Exploration, and Conquest

primary_sources: Bartolomé de las Casas, A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies (1542)

options.text: Spanish crown laws limiting abuses in the encomienda system

options.misconception: The debate made Spain give up its colonies.
options.text: Spain abandoned all of its colonies in the Americas

options.misconception: The debate ended English colonization.
options.text: England ended its colonization of North America

options.misconception: The debate gave Indigenous peoples full political equality.
options.text: Indigenous peoples gained full political equality in New Spain

rationales.A: Background: pressure from Las Casas helped bring the New Laws of 1542, which tried to limit abuses in the encomienda system.
rationales.B: Spain kept its colonies; it did not abandon them.
rationales.C: England expanded its colonization; it did not end it.
rationales.D: No political equality for Indigenous peoples followed.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what a debate like this could change. A critic who reaches the crown can push for new laws.
2. Name the result. Background: the New Laws of 1542 tried to limit encomienda abuses.
3. Test the other options. Spain kept its colonies, England kept colonizing, and no equality followed.
4. Keep the scale honest. A law limiting abuse is a real result, not a revolution.
Remember: a reform debate usually produces a law, not the end of an empire.

books.section: Topic 1.4 Columbian Exchange, Spanish Exploration, and Conquest

primary_sources: Bartolomé de las Casas, A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies (1542)

options.misconception: The passage shows how Indigenous peoples worshipped day to day.
options.text: The daily religious practices of Indigenous peoples before contact

options.misconception: The passage can be used to count the population in 1492.
options.text: The population size of Indigenous communities in 1492
A Spanish critic’s perspective on conquest and its effects

options.misconception: The passage shows how Indigenous peoples fought back.
options.text: The military strategies used by Indigenous peoples against Spain

rationales.A: The excerpt does not document daily religious practices.
rationales.B: A polemical account alone cannot establish a population size.
rationales.C: The passage is most useful as a Spanish critic's perspective on conquest, shaped by his religious position and his purpose of reform.
rationales.D: Las Casas does not describe Indigenous military strategies.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what the source is. A Spanish friar writing to condemn conquest.
2. Ask what that position lets the source show. A critic's view of what conquest did, not a neutral record.
3. Test the other uses. Daily worship, population size, and military strategy are not in the passage.
4. Name the use. It is evidence for how one Spaniard saw conquest and its effects.
Remember: a source's use depends on who wrote it and why, not only on what it says.

primary_sources: Contemporary accounts of Bacon’s Rebellion (1676), paraphrased

options.misconception: The tension was between the governor and Parliament.
options.text: Conflict between royal governors and the British Parliament over taxation

options.misconception: The tension was between Anglicans and Puritans.
options.text: Conflict between Anglican clergy and Puritan dissenters over church governance
Conflict between former indentured servants seeking land and wealthy planters

options.misconception: The tension was between enslaved Africans and Indigenous nations.
options.text: Conflict between enslaved Africans and Indigenous nations over trade routes

rationales.A: The conflict is between small farmers and planters, not between a governor and Parliament.
rationales.B: No religious conflict over church governance appears in the excerpt.
rationales.C: The excerpt centers on land hunger and taxes: former servants and small farmers against wealthy planters who monopolized land and government.
rationales.D: Enslaved Africans and Indigenous nations are not the parties in this rebellion.
rationales.general:
1. List what the people complain about. No land, heavy taxes, and a few men holding everything.
2. Name the two sides. Former indentured servants seeking land against wealthy planters who control it.
3. Check the other pairs. Governors and Parliament, Anglicans and Puritans, enslaved people and Indigenous nations are not the parties here.
4. Match the tension to the complaint. Land and taxes point to servants against planters.
Remember: match the complaint to the people who voice it, not to any conflict from the period.

examOnly.source: original; stimulus is a paraphrase of contemporary accounts of Bacon’s Rebellion (1676)
examOnly.stem: The discontent described in the excerpt most directly reflected which of the following tensions in colonial Virginia?

stimulus.source_note: Account of Bacon’s Rebellion in Virginia, 1676, paraphrased from contemporary reports.
stimulus.text: We have found that the people are discontented because they are kept from land and are forced to pay heavy taxes while a few engross all. The people have taken up arms against those who oppress them.

primary_sources: Contemporary accounts of Bacon’s Rebellion (1676), paraphrased

options.misconception: The rebellion ended the House of Burgesses.
options.text: Virginia abolished the House of Burgesses

options.misconception: The rebellion won voting rights for all free men.
options.text: Virginia granted voting rights to all free men regardless of property

options.misconception: The rebellion ended tobacco farming.
options.text: Virginia ended tobacco cultivation in favor of wheat farming
Virginia planters increasingly turned to enslaved African labor

rationales.A: The House of Burgesses continued; it was not abolished.
rationales.B: No broad expansion of voting rights followed the rebellion.
rationales.C: Tobacco remained central; Virginia did not switch to wheat.
rationales.D: Background: after the rebellion, planters distrusted a large class of armed, landless former servants and shifted toward enslaved African labor, which they saw as more controllable.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what frightened the planters. An armed uprising by landless former servants.
2. Ask what labor they would trust instead. Background: they turned to enslaved African labor, which they saw as more controllable.
3. Test the other options. The Burgesses continued, no suffrage followed, and tobacco stayed central.
4. Connect fear to consequence. The rebellion pushed planters toward labor they could control.
Remember: a rebellion's consequence lies in how the powerful respond, not in what the rebels won.

stimulus.source_note: Account of Bacon’s Rebellion in Virginia, 1676, paraphrased from contemporary reports.
stimulus.text: We have found that the people are discontented because they are kept from land and are forced to pay heavy taxes while a few engross all. The people have taken up arms against those who oppress them.

primary_sources: Contemporary accounts of Bacon’s Rebellion (1676), paraphrased

options.text: The growing willingness of colonists to challenge established political authority

options.misconception: The rebellion ended conflict with Indigenous peoples.
options.text: The steady decline of conflict between colonists and Indigenous peoples

options.misconception: The rebellion weakened ties to the Atlantic economy.
options.text: The weakening of ties between the colonies and the Atlantic economy

options.misconception: The rebellion spread religious tolerance in the South.
options.text: The spread of religious tolerance throughout the Southern colonies

rationales.A: Bacon's Rebellion is an early example of colonists organizing against established authority, a pattern that recurs through the Revolution. The rebels were landless former servants demanding land and a voice, not a foreign enemy.
rationales.B: Conflict with Indigenous peoples continued; it did not decline.
rationales.C: Atlantic ties deepened; they did not weaken.
rationales.D: The Southern colonies remained religiously restrictive.
rationales.general:
1. Name the pattern. Colonists took up arms against those who governed them.
2. Ask whether the pattern repeats. Colonists challenged established authority again and again, into the Revolution.
3. Test the other continuities. Conflict with Indigenous peoples went on, Atlantic ties deepened, and the South stayed restrictive.
4. Keep the claim narrow. One rebellion shows a willingness to challenge authority, not a change in everything.
Remember: a continuity is a pattern that repeats, not a single event.

options.misconception: The Salem trials were a parallel revolt over land.
options.text: The Salem witch trials in Massachusetts
The Pueblo Revolt against Spanish rule in New Mexico

options.misconception: Georgia's founding paralleled the rebellion.
options.text: The establishment of Georgia as a debtor colony

options.misconception: Pennsylvania's founding paralleled the rebellion.
options.text: The founding of Pennsylvania as a refuge for Quakers

rationales.A: The Salem witch trials were a religious panic, not a revolt over land and authority.
rationales.B: Background: the Pueblo Revolt of 1680 was also a revolt against oppressive colonial rule, fought for land and autonomy, though by Indigenous peoples against Spain.
rationales.C: Georgia's founding was a colony's beginning, not a rebellion.
rationales.D: Pennsylvania's founding was a refuge's beginning, not a rebellion.
rationales.general:
1. Name the grievance. People denied land and taxed heavily, rising against their oppressors.
2. Look for the same grievance elsewhere. Background: the Pueblo Revolt of 1680 was also a revolt against oppressive colonial rule over land and autonomy.
3. Test the other options. Salem was a panic; Georgia and Pennsylvania were foundings, not revolts.
4. Match the shape. A revolt over land and authority parallels another over land and authority.
Remember: a parallel matches the grievance and the action, not just the century.
